name: Frequent small meals

card.summary: Eating five to seven spaced meals a day, a bodybuilding habit used to support muscle gain and keep body fat in check for a fuller, leaner physique.
card.note: Reviews of controlled trials find meal frequency matters less than total intake; some lifters report preferring fewer meals.

quick.overview:
Frequent small meals means spreading food across five to seven eating occasions rather than three large ones. It is a long-standing bodybuilding habit, built on the idea that regular protein and calories keep muscle building going and appetite controlled, which supports a bigger, leaner physique.

Research on meal frequency is mixed. Sports nutrition position statements focus on total intake and protein distribution, and reviews of meal timing report small or inconsistent differences in body composition between patterns [1][2][3].
quick.how: Lifters typically portion their daily food into evenly spaced meals, often including protein at each, and prepare food ahead. T Nation training logs show some adopting the pattern from diet books built on never going hungry [4].
quick.risks: The pattern itself is low-risk, but some lifters report it does not suit them; one forum user said it did not agree with their metabolism and now prefers fasting [5]. Frequent eating can be inconvenient and may make appetite harder to manage for some people.

lead: Frequent small meals is the practice of eating five to seven times a day. In bodybuilding and fitness culture it is used to keep protein and calories steady for muscle growth and to avoid long gaps that followers think could slow progress [4].

Nutrient-timing research has examined whether the distribution of protein and carbohydrate through the day affects recovery, muscle protein synthesis and body composition. The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand summarises that timing can influence recovery and muscle protein synthesis for trained people [1]. Reviews of meal frequency and timing report limited or inconsistent effects on weight and metabolic markers, and a thermic-effect review notes evidence that larger meals produce a larger post-meal energy rise than frequent small ones [2][3][6].
A 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials of at least 12 weeks examined meal timing strategies, including reduced meal frequency, and their effects on body measurements and metabolic markers [7].

chain: Spread protein and calories across 5-7 meals
Steady supply for training and recovery; appetite kept regular
More muscle gain and easier fat control
angle.text: Lifters use the pattern to hit daily protein and calorie targets and support training, which in turn builds muscle and manages body fat. The effect on looks arrives through total intake and training rather than through the meal count itself.

paras: The pattern divides daily intake into several smaller meals. Snacking reviews note that many studies suggest distributing energy across four to five eating occasions could favourably affect health, and that snack composition matters [8].

The ISSN nutrient-timing position stand discusses spacing protein and carbohydrate around exercise for recovery and muscle protein synthesis in trained people [1]. A 2023 study reported that the muscle anabolic response to protein ingestion after exercise shows no upper limit in magnitude or duration, a point sometimes raised in discussions of how much protein can be used per meal [9].

The American Heart Association statement on meal timing reviewed breakfast skipping, intermittent fasting and meal frequency for cardiometabolic health [10]. A thermic-effect review reports that larger meals, rather than frequent small ones, are associated with a bigger post-meal metabolic rise [3]. A systematic review of intermittent fasting trials found weight loss comparable to calorie restriction [6].
On T Nation, lifters describe frequent small meals as part of programmes that stress never being hungry [4], while others report moving to fasting after finding the pattern did not suit them [5].

Controlled trials and reviews have compared meal frequency and timing on weight and metabolic outcomes, with small or inconsistent differences in many analyses [2][3][6][7]. Sports nutrition statements address timing around training [1].

timeline.event: ISSN publishes a position stand on nutrient timing [1]; the AHA issues a statement on meal timing and frequency [10].
A JAMA Network Open meta-analysis assesses meal timing strategies of 12 weeks or more [7].
